summary: Addresses the IETF and RFC Editor rule that a document cannot be published until everything it normatively references is at the same maturity level or higher. That rule sometimes caused long delays. This best current practice relaxes it for references to standards-track documents.

plainLanguage.summary: A rule said you cannot finish your homework until every book you mention is also finished. This note says some books can still be in progress when you finish.

questions: what is note and move on in ietf
subtitle: The 'note and move on' rule: publish now and annotate references to less mature standards-track documents.

tldr.problem: A long-standing rule held a document back until every document it normatively referenced reached the same maturity level or higher, causing very long publication delays.
tldr.mechanism: For published Standards-Track and BCP targets, the author keeps the reference and adds a note that the target is of lower maturity and may be less stable, then publication proceeds.
tldr.outcome: It is a simpler alternative to the exception procedure in RFC 3967, which still applies for other classes of documents, and it updates RFC 3967 by recommending the same annotations there.

today: RFC 4897 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 3967. The metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes it or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem With the Old Rule
sections.content:
The IETF and RFC Editor have a long-standing rule (see RFC 2026, Section 4.2.4, and the discussion in RFC 3967) that a document at a given maturity level cannot be published until all documents it makes a normative reference to are at that level or higher.

The rule sometimes caused very long publication delays, and there were claims it was a major obstruction to advancing documents. RFC 3967 added an exception for normative downward references in specific circumstances, but its fairly stringent requirements did not clear the backlog or stop new documents joining the queue.

RFC 4897 replaces the rule for downward references to Standards-Track documents, including BCPs, that are already published. Instead of holding the newer document, the author can note the downward reference and move on.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule made people wait a very long time for their friends' work to be done. The new rule says you can go ahead if you leave a note.

sections.title: Source and Target Documents
sections.content:
A reference involves two documents. The source document is the one holding the reference, and the target document is the one referenced.

In this specification, the term Standards-Track document includes BCPs but not Informational or Experimental documents of any variety or origin.
sections.plainLanguage: The source is the book you are writing. The target is the book you mention inside it.

sections.title: The Note-and-Move-On Procedure
sections.content:
An author who needs a normative downward reference to a Standards-Track RFC writes the reference as usual in the Normative References section. Then a note is added to the reference text saying that the target is of a lower maturity level, that some caution is advised since it may be less stable than the referencing document, and, optionally, why the downward reference is appropriate.

The Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) may specify the exact wording, set procedures or give guidance, and should seek community review when setting procedures. The annotations are part of the source document, so anyone can object to the reference or the note at any time in the document life cycle. There is no separate review of these references.

With community review the IESG may set rules for when a downward reference should delay a document and when it should just be noted. Absent such guidance, authors and reviewers use their best judgment, on the assumption that in a significant majority of cases noting is preferable to delaying. Authors may also attach similar notes to non-normative references.
sections.plainLanguage: Write the name of the unfinished book, and add a sticky note: this one may still change, be careful. Then you can hand in your homework.

sections.title: Documents Already Waiting and Non-Standards-Track Targets
sections.content:
For source documents already in the RFC Editor queue, the IESG may specify a procedure. It should encourage authors whose documents are waiting on downward references to Standards-Track RFCs to consider whether the new rule suits them. If the authors think adding an annotation and releasing is best, the IESG should ensure appropriate review and, if that review agrees, allow the annotations to be added. The IESG announces its decision through the normal Protocol-Action or Document-Action mechanisms.

For normative references to documents that are not on the standards track and are approved under RFC 3967, the same annotation (or the retrospective annotation for queued documents) SHOULD be added, unless the IESG, after considering Last Call input, concludes it is inappropriate. This is the sense in which RFC 4897 updates RFC 3967.
sections.plainLanguage: Homework already stuck in the waiting pile can also get the sticky note, if the teachers agree. Even the special-case books from the older rule should get a note.

sections.title: What Can Be Referenced This Way
sections.content:
The downward reference by annotation model applies only to published Standards-Track RFCs at lower maturity levels. These references are part of the source document at IETF Last Call, so the community can comment on them.

Advancing the target document, when appropriate, is still considered preferable to using either this procedure or the one in RFC 3967. The RFC sets no specific test of appropriateness, because it would be impossible in the general case and because the aim is to let the IESG and the community weigh the importance of publishing the source document against the time and difficulty of upgrading the target. The requirement is intended to be less stringent than that of RFC 3967.
sections.plainLanguage: Finishing the other book is still the best choice. The sticky note is just a way to avoid waiting forever when that is not practical.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document specifies an IETF procedure and is not believed to raise any security issues. It adds one caution: in principle, relaxing the downward-reference rules for references associated with security mechanisms could make a specification less stable and hence less secure.
sections.plainLanguage: If the unfinished book is about locks, relying on it could make things less safe, so take extra care.

references.text: Bradner, S., "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3", BCP 9, RFC 2026, October 1996.
Bush, R. and T. Narten, "Clarifying when Standards Track Documents may Refer Normatively to Documents at a Lower Level", BCP 97, RFC 3967, December 2004.
